identification.title: Agnus Dei
identification.notes: Written by Michael W. Smith alone; PraiseCharts gives the copyright as 1990 Milene Music, administered by Sony/ATV. The list's artist guess is right. It first appeared on Smith's 1990 pop-leaning album Go West Young Man and became a congregational standard after his 2001 live Worship recording. This is Smith's song, not the Latin liturgical Agnus Dei, though both take their title from John 1:29. A commenter on one review confuses it with Samuel Barber's unrelated piece of the same name; the credit to Smith is not in doubt. CCLI number not confirmed from a source read for this review.

claims.structuralNotes: One short verse of praise, sung twice, each time followed by the same two-part chorus, with a closing amen; no bridge. The verse calls for alleluia because the Lord God Almighty reigns. The chorus is addressed to God, declaring him holy and the Lamb worthy. The Lamb is named by title only. It narrates no act of God: no cross, resurrection or return is stated, and the sacrifice is carried by the title and the Scripture behind it. The voice is credal, with no singular first person.

claims.claim: The Lord God Almighty reigns, and that is a cause for praise.
claims.subject: The sovereign reign of God

claims.claim: The Lord God Almighty is holy.
claims.subject: The holiness of God

strengths.title: The Lamb is named and worshipped
strengths.explanation: Christ is addressed under his sacrificial title and declared worthy, with no hedging about whom the praise is for. The song does not narrate the atonement; the title points to it for those who know John 1:29.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world - the title the song is built on.

strengths.title: The throne-room worship of Revelation
strengths.explanation: The song takes the heavenly acclamation of the holy God and the worthy Lamb and puts it in the congregation's mouth. That is worship shaped by Scripture rather than by mood.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive honour and glory - the acclamation the song borrows.

doctrinesAffirmed: The worthiness of Christ the Lamb
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. A brief, scriptural song of adoration built on the acclamations of Revelation 19, 4 and 5. It declares God's reign, his holiness and the Lamb's worth, and names no act: the cross, resurrection and return are not stated, and the Lamb title carries the sacrifice only through Scripture's background. That is a limit of scope, not an error.

strengths.title: Short and easy to hold
strengths.explanation: The text is tiny and the movement repeats, so a room that has never heard it can join within a pass. It suits a time of quiet adoration or a response to the Word.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published in several keys; no chart was read. Test the entry point with your own room, since the original recording suits a trained voice.

range.key: Not verified; published in multiple keys
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The text is only a few short lines, repeated several times over. The repetition dwells on scriptural acclamations, but it also does the work of length: little further is said after the first pass.
communal.assessment: Congregational in words and form: brief, easy to learn, and addressed to God. It works as a response of adoration after the Word or at communion and does not depend on a lead vocal.

strengths.title: The Lamb and the Lord God Almighty are named
strengths.explanation: There is no vague addressee. The song names the holy God and the Lamb, and anyone who knows the Bible knows who is meant.

clarity.assessment: Clear to a churchgoer. An outsider might not recognise the Lamb as Jesus: the song leans on the congregation's knowledge of John 1 and Revelation and does not explain itself.

synthesis.summary: A very short song of adoration: the Lord God Almighty reigns, he is holy, and the Lamb is worthy, taking the acclamations of Revelation 19, 4 and 5 into the congregation's mouth. Christ is named by title only. No act of God is narrated, so the atonement is carried by the title alone, and the thin text is stretched by repetition. No false claims.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin - the title of the song.
The holiness acclaimed of the Lord God Almighty by the living creatures.
The Lamb who was slain is worthy - the acclamation the song borrows.
